props.title: Prime Cut

sections.content: **Prime Cut** (1972) stands as a gritty, unflinching neo-noir that captures America's heartland darkness through Lee Marvin's steely performance as Nick Devlin, a Chicago enforcer confronting Gene Hackman's ruthless meat-packing kingpin. Director Michael Ritchie crafts a disturbing portrait of Midwest corruption that feels spiritually connected to other cynical '70s crime films like Point Blank (1967) and Get Carter (1971). The film's brutal metaphors comparing human trafficking to cattle slaughter created controversy, but its unflinching examination of exploitation and violence in America's heartland makes it a vital entry in '70s neo-noir.

sections.content: The film's stark violence and moral ambiguity exemplifies the gritty realism that defined New Hollywood crime films of the early 1970s. Like The French Connection (1971) and **Charley Varrick** (1973), **Prime Cut** strips away glamorous crime movie conventions to expose America's underbelly. Ritchie's documentary-like approach to filming the Kansas locations adds a layer of authenticity that makes the film's brutality even more unsettling.

Lee Marvin's controlled performance as Nick Devlin follows the template of the professional criminal antihero that he helped establish in Point Blank (1967). But here, the character's moral code provides the only sense of order in a corrupt rural landscape. The film shares DNA with other "city criminal in hostile territory" narratives like Walking Tall (1973) and **Rolling Thunder** (1977), though **Prime Cut**'s political subtext cuts deeper. sections.content: **Prime Cut** helped establish a subgenre of rural noir that would influence films like **Southern Comfort** (1981) and **Blood Simple** (1984). Its unflinching look at heartland corruption challenged the romanticized view of rural America, much like **Bad Day at Black Rock** (1955) did in the previous generation. The film's metaphorical connection between meat processing and human exploitation creates a devastating critique of American capitalism that feels prescient today.
